## Recovery Still Proving to be Patchy 



- This is the last issue of this monitor and over the more than ten years that it has been published the cable industry has been through many changes. The most dramatic has been the slump that started in Q4 2008 and despite the fact that the recovery has been underway for almost a year now, this remains very fragile. Whilst some sectors, such as winding wire, have rebounded quite strongly, others, such as construction cables, still have some pain to come, and the spectre of a further slowdown has not completely gone away. 



- Initial data shows that in H1 global copper wirerod and wire and cable production grew by 6.6% year-on-year, with the growth rate moderating in Q2 to 5.7% after a rise of 7.6% in Q1. The main driver continues to be Asia, with Europe and North America only posting growth of around 2% in terms of wirerod consumption in H1. This leaves H1 wirerod consumption still 5.4% below H1 2008 and 3.7% below H1 2007, and it will not be until 2011 at best that the global market gets back to pre-crisis levels. 

As editor of this monitor for most of its life I would like to thank all our subscribers for their support and wish you well for the future. I would also like to remind people that data on the wirerod and wire and cable markets covered by this publication will continue to be available, with the rod data in the _CRU Copper Monitor_ and the wire and cable data in the _Cables Industry Analyst_ newsletter.

© 2010 CRU International Ltd **confidential** Page 3 of 12 July 2010 Copper wire, cable and wirerod **www.crugroup.com** # Europe ### **Production exhibits y-o-y recovery and seasonal sequential growth** According to our estimates European copper and cable output reached 601,000t in Q2 2010. The figure was up by 3% compared to year ago levels. It was also up sequentially by 13%. Winding wire, which was the strongest segment, rose by 22% y-o-y to 118,000t in Q2 2010. This is mainly attributed to the recovery in the automotive and consumer goods sectors. Energy and communication cables were down y-o-y to 409,000t and 74,000t from 414,000t and 72,000t respectively. The construction sector in Europe continues to be under pressure whilst infrastructure projects have been impacted by ailing public finances. Initial estimates show that copper wirerod production in Europe amounted to 753,000t in Q2 2010, up by 3% y-o-y and 10% sequentially. Germany remained the largest national producer with output of 186,000t in Q2, an increase of 4% y-o-y. **Aurubis** reported that it is producing copper wirerod at 80-90% utilisation level. The company remains optimistic regarding the market until the end of the year. Italian wirerod output also rose in Q2, to 119,000t from 110,000t a year ago. French output fell by 34% y-o-y to 46,000t; this is attributed to the closure of **Nexans’** plant in Chauny. Also, Spanish output grew by 8% to 88,000t in Q2 2010. ### **Industry restructuring affects trade patterns** European copper wirerod trade rose by 9% y-o-y to almost 400,000t in Q1 2010. In the same period, Western European exports surged by 18% to 290,000t, significantly supported by a weak euro. Furthermore, the closure of the Chauny plant impacted trade dramatically. French wirerod exports fell by 23% in Q1 2010 whilst imports surged by 41%. German exports increased by 17% to just under 100,000t. Exports from Belgium soared by 40% to 53,000t. In addition, Spanish exports saw strong growth of 44% to 39,000t, largely attributed to new capacity installed by **La Farga Group,** coupled with the poor home market. ### **Tales from a heavily indebted market place** The two-speed recovery mode in Europe is now more evident than ever, exacerbated by the sovereign debt crisis. Germany continues to lead the way, with copper wire and cable consumption in Q2 having grown by an estimated 12% to 149,000t. In

addition, the French market grew by 3% y-o-y to 59,000t in the same period whilst the Benelux market saw a 19% increase to 36,000t. But the heavily indebted public finances in the South have impacted demand for wire and cable products. Whilst the construction sector remains depressed, projects financed by national government investment programmes are in danger too due to the recently announced austerity measures. During the financial crisis in late 2008 and the greatest part of 2009, large projects, mainly consuming power cable, provided significant support to the European wire and cable industry, especially at a time when private investment was squeezed. But considering the ailing public finances revealed in 2010, the less efficient wire and cable manufacturers will be challenged and CRU anticipates that this may lead to further industry restructuring and consolidation in Southern Europe. The Italian copper wire and cable market fell by 1% to 57,000t in Q2 whilst the Spanish remained flat at 51,000t. Other W. Europe (which includes the heavily troubled Greece and Portugal) contracted by 5% y-o-y to 67,000t. ector and also an upturn in the production of domestic appliances. In the first five months of 2010 production of all major appliances was up by 2.5% compared to the same period in 2009, with output of refrigerators up by 18.4% meaning strong demand for compressor motors. The air conditioning sector remains the weakest with production of room air conditioners and dehumidifiers down by 6.5%. After a slow start to the year, which saw appliance production fall year-on-year in both January and February, the following three months saw a sustained return to growth, which is the first time there has been three consecutive months of growth since 2007. North American vehicle production is up 67.6% in the first five months of 2010 compared to the same period in 2009, with similar growth in each of the three countries. The only sector where growth is muted is in medium and heavy trucks, where output is only up by 18.9%. ### **But the construction sector remains weak** The Architecture Billings Index, a leading indicator of US non-residential construction, fell to 45.8 from 48.4 in the previous month. Banks continue to be cautious about extending credit, and this is negatively impacting construction projects. The fall in the index indicates that non-residential construction activity is likely to continue to contract for at least the next 6 - 9 months. In the residential sector housing starts had been rising modestly, but in May they were down 10% to an annual rate of 574,000 and applications for building permits were down by 5.9% to 610,000. Withdrawal of government tax credits are being blamed for the fall, which illustrates the fragile nature of any recovery in the housing sector, with the May figure for starts being the lowest for any month this year. It now looks increasingly certain that there will be no significant upturn in demand for wire and cable from the construction sector in 2010. ### **Outlook continues to be fragile** The US economy has suffered some setbacks and disappointments recently. On the other hand the recovery in manufacturing continues apace. What this tells us is that the recovery overall remains fragile and hesitant. Retail sales fell 1.2% month-on-month in May, reversing seven months of sequential gains. They remain up almost 4.5% on the year, but still prone to wobbles, and as a result consumer spending is unlikely to resume pole position in the economy any time soon. The problem for households is that two pillars of their spending – the health of the labour market, and personal wealth – remain under considerable pressure. a 12% sequential increase.  Regional copper wire and cable output reached 377,000t in Q2 2010, up by 13% from year ago levels and 9% from the previous quarter.  Copper wire and cable consumption totalled an estimated 370,000t in Q2 2010. Winding wire recovered strongly, rising by 51% y-o-y to 86,000t supported by a robust rebound from its end-use segments.  With a regional market of 246,000t in Q2, energy cable is the largest product segment. With growth of just 7% y-o-y this sector showed the slowest growth due to continued poor demand from the construction industry. 

### **Japan continues to grow** 

According to the **Japanese Electric Wire and Cable Makers’ Association** , copper wire and cable shipments increased by 11% y-o-y to 49,700t in May 2010.  That was the fifth straight month of y-o-y gains.  However, shipments were down by 12% from 56,200t in April.  The association is anticipating that shipments in full FY 2010 will reach 661,000t, on a par with FY 2009.  According to our estimates, Japanese use of copper wirerod in wire and cable was 165,000t in Q2 2010.  This represents a 17% y-o-y increase, supported by recovered markets for automobiles and consumer goods which were depressed in H1 2009.  From a q-o-q point of view, Q2 2010 was up by 5.4%.  Copper wirerod output reached an estimated 178,000t in Q2 2010, up by 10% compared to the same period in 2009.  Sequentially, the figure was up by 9%.  Our estimates indicate that magnet wire output was 43,000t in Q2 2010, up from 24,000t in Q2 2009.  Copper power cable production fell by an estimated 10% y-o-y to 43,000t in Q2 2010. 

### **South Korean growth now lagging its neighbours** 

Copper wirerod production in South Korea is estimated to have increased by 4% y-o-y to 192,000t in Q2 2010.  Compared with the previous quarter, production rose by 9%.  Consumption of copper wirerod is estimated to have reached 149,000t in Q2 2010, a 7% increase both y-o-y and sequentially.  A similar trend is followed by copper wirerod used in wire and cable products.  Our estimates indicate that this reached 132,000t in Q2 2010, up by 7% y-o-y and 8% q-o-q. 

### **Taiwan has a good H1** 

Taiwanese production of copper wirerod reached an estimated 105,000t in Q2 2010.  The number was up by 9% from year ago levels.  Compared with the previous quarter, wirerod output soared by 24%. Wirerod consumption also saw significant sequential growth of 23% to 88,000t in Q2.  Compared to the same period in 2009 the figure increased by 9%.  Our data shows that output of copper wire and cable used in electronic applications rose by almost 50% y-o-y to 22,400t, driven by a robust recovery in electronics goods.  Power cable production increased by only 2.5% to 59,100t as this end-use segment continues to be impacted by the severe global downturn felt in 2009, taking longer to recover than other product segments such as winding wire.

part due to the weak Q1 2009, the rate of growth slowed in Q2, but we still expect growth for the whole of 2010 to be in the high single digit range. China’s economy continues to grow quite strongly, but wage rates are rising, with minimum wages having recently been raised by 15-25% in the coastal regions in response to growing worker unrest. However, higher wages should help boost local consumption and should increase demand for electrical appliances. Demand for power cable has slowed due to a reduction in grid investment, with output down by 5-10% in the months of March, April and May, but the real estate sector is strong due to government action in doubling the area of land sales for property development and targeting the building of three million social housing units. The impact of the stimulus package announced in Q2 2009 is also having an impact now due to the lag between projects being planned and cable being needed. 

A recent survey of 20 copper wire and cable producers showed an operating capacity utilisation rate of 78.5% in April and 83.3% in May, and in talking to manufacturers we get the impression that rates have continued to improve slightly in June. There are some worries that government curbs to limit inflation and stop the economy overheating will have an impact on cable demand, but most producers seem to be of the view that steady growth will continue in the second half of this year. There are though some worries that the building wire market will be negatively impacted in the middle of 2011 as a result of stricter controls on the real estate market that have recently been introduced. 

### **North African market is growing quite strongly** 

One sign of the strength of the North African market is the growth in wire and cable imports, with trade generally correlating quite closely with demand. In Morocco metallic cable imports in Q1 2010 were 32.2% up in volume on Q1 2009, with Spain, France, Portugal and China being the main source of these imports. Imports into Tunisia have grown even more quickly, rising by just over 100% year-on-year in Q1 2010. Over half of these imports are from France and Germany, and an important driver for this is the growing production of automotive harnesses as well as a healthy local market. A number of companies are relocating harness production operations from Eastern Europe to Tunisia and whilst some of the automotive wire used is made locally, a significant volume is being imported. For Algeria the growth in imports has been more modest at 6.1%, but unlike Morocco and Tunisia there had been no dip in 2009, so this figure is over 50% up on Q1 2008. Growth in the Algerian market has been slowed a little by the fall in gas prices, but the government here still has big plans to upgrade the country’s infrastructure and this will require large volumes of wire and cable. It will make both AC and DC cables and will cost US$90m, employing around 100 people. As of now the site for this factory is still under consideration. China’s **Tianjin Huabei Group** will commission its new 400,000 tpy copper rod unit in the second half of 2010. This line has been imported from the US. **Hitachi Cable** is planning on investing US$33-44m in building an industrial cables plant in Northern Vietnam. The aim is to have the plant in production by 2012. Korean cable manufacturer **Taihan** has sold its 9.9% stake in Prysmian for US$348m, which seems to put an end to any speculation about a possible tie up between the two companies. **Sumitomo Electric** is talking to a number of European vehicle manufacturers about the possible use of more aluminium wiring. Meanwhile the company has begun commercial production of aluminium automotive wiring harness. Swedish cable manufacturer **Habia Cable** is to relocate production of telecom products, including cable, from its Soderfors plant in Sweden to China.
